track.name: startup-finance
track.label: Startup Finance & Unit Economics
track.summary: Master the financial language of startups — from burn rate and runway to CAC/LTV, fundraising term sheets, SaaS metrics, and cap table mechanics that founders and operators need to grow with confidence.

phases.title: Startup Accounting Basics
phases.description: Build the financial foundation every startup operator needs — understand the three core statements, accrual vs cash accounting, and the financial structure that supports growth.

phases.title: Unit Economics & CAC/LTV
phases.description: Learn to calculate customer acquisition cost and lifetime value, interpret the LTV:CAC ratio, and use unit economics to decide when a business model is actually working.

phases.title: Runway & Cash Management
phases.description: Track burn rate, extend runway, manage working capital, and build the cash flow models that keep a startup solvent through the gaps between funding rounds.

phases.title: Fundraising Mechanics & Term Sheets
phases.description: Understand the funding stages from pre-seed to Series A, decode a term sheet, and evaluate SAFEs and convertible notes before signing anything.

phases.title: SaaS Metrics & Revenue Models
phases.description: Master the SaaS metrics dashboard — ARR, MRR, churn, net revenue retention, and the benchmarks investors use to evaluate recurring revenue businesses.

phases.title: Cap Table & Equity Compensation
phases.description: Model a cap table through multiple funding rounds, understand dilution and the option pool shuffle, and design employee stock option plans that attract top talent.

topics.title: Choosing a Revenue Model and a First Price
topics.description: The decision unit economics assumes you already made: what you charge for, how often, and how much.

steps.t: Write down what the customer is buying
steps.d: A seat, a transaction, a volume of usage, an outcome, or access. The unit you pick decides every metric downstream.

steps.t: Compare three models on one whiteboard
steps.d: Subscription, usage-based and a one-off fee for the same product. Note which one a big customer prefers and which one you can forecast.

steps.t: Set a price and charge it
steps.d: Pick a defensible number and invoice someone. What people pay tells you more in a week than surveys do in a month.

steps.t: Work out the unit economics of that choice
steps.d: Cost to acquire one customer against gross margin over their life. Do it per model — usage-based and subscription behave differently.

steps.t: Decide what would make you change
steps.d: Write the signal in advance: churn above X, or customers repeatedly asking to pay a different way. Pricing is a lever, not a one-time decision.

topics.title: Startup Accounting Fundamentals
topics.description: Learn how accrual accounting differs from cash accounting, why startups use both, and what your accountant actually does each month.

steps.d: Show how an invoice sent in December but paid in January is recorded in December under accrual (revenue) but January under cash (cash received).
Take a $50k expense incurred but unpaid, and record it under cash accounting (no impact until paid) and accrual (impact immediately).

steps.t: Show the impact on a case study
steps.d: Take a startup that invoiced $100k in December but received payment in January, and show on a P&L and cash flow how accrual records the revenue immediately while cash accounting shows it in January.
Walk through a month: record transactions, accrue payables and receivables, depreciate assets, close books, then produce financial statements.
Reconcile a bank account to accounting records, verify that all expenses and revenue are recorded, and confirm balance sheet ties to cash.

topics.title: P&L, Balance Sheet & Cash Flow
topics.description: Read the three core financial statements as an operator — understand what each one tells you about the health and trajectory of your business.

steps.d: Create a spreadsheet with a P&L (revenue - expenses = profit), a balance sheet (assets = liabilities + equity), and a cash flow (operating + investing + financing).

steps.t: Analyze P&L metrics for two startups
steps.d: Compare the P&Ls of a SaaS and marketplace startup, noting differences in gross margin, operating leverage, and net income, to see how business model shapes the statement.
Describe what cash, receivables, payables, and debt mean and how each affects runway; for example, $1M in receivables means cash is tied up.
Explain why a profitable company can still run out of cash if cash inflows lag expenses, and how to spot this from the statement.
For a startup, identify red flags (negative cash flow, high burn, receivables growing faster than revenue) and green flags (improving gross margin, strong cash conversion).

topics.title: Financial Structure for Startups
topics.description: Set up a chart of accounts, choose the right entity type, and understand the financial infrastructure that makes reporting and fundraising easier.

steps.d: Set up GL buckets for revenue, cost of goods, operating expenses (grouped by function), interest, and taxes, so monthly reports are consistent and comparable.
Decide between a C-corp (separate tax entity, required for VC), an LLC (pass-through taxation), or a Delaware C-corp (standard for venture).
Choose accounting software (QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite) and supporting tools (Expensify for expense reports, Brex for corporate card) to automate close.

steps.t: Set up a bank account structure
steps.d: Create operating, payroll, and tax reserve accounts to separate cash purposes and make reconciliation easier.
Write a one-page guide on revenue recognition (when do you record an invoice?), expense accrual (payables, bonuses, taxes), and depreciation so others follow the same rules.

topics.title: Calculating CAC and LTV
topics.description: Compute blended and channel-level customer acquisition cost and lifetime value — and understand why the ratio between them determines business model viability.

steps.d: Divide total marketing spend by new customers acquired to get cost per customer; do this monthly to track whether unit economics improve or worsen.
For each channel (paid search, sales team, referral, organic), calculate CAC separately to identify which channel scales and which is expensive.
For a subscription business, LTV = (average monthly revenue per customer - monthly churn rate) / (monthly churn rate); for e-commerce, use total gross margin per customer.
Explain that LTV:CAC > 3:1 means your business is sustainable, < 1:1 means you lose money per customer, and between 1:1 and 3:1 means growth but profitability depends on CAC payback.
Track CAC and LTV by cohort over 12 months to see whether recent cohorts have better or worse economics than earlier ones.

topics.title: CAC Payback Period
topics.description: Calculate how many months of gross margin it takes to recover what you spent to acquire a customer — a key signal for capital efficiency and growth sustainability.

steps.d: For a SaaS company, calculate months to payback = (CAC) / (monthly gross margin per customer) to see how long until the customer recoups their acquisition cost.
Calculate payback separately for each marketing channel to identify which channel has fastest payback and therefore best capital efficiency.
Explain that a 6-month payback means half the customer's useful life is spent recovering CAC; longer payback means slower cash recovery and higher funding needs.
Show that a $2M burn and $10k monthly CAC implies 20 customers/month burn, while faster payback means you can scale longer on same capital.
Compare your payback to SaaS benchmarks (typically 12-18 months) to assess whether your unit economics are competitive.

topics.title: Unit Economics for Non-SaaS Models
topics.description: Adapt the CAC/LTV framework to marketplace, e-commerce, and transactional models where contribution margin per order replaces monthly recurring revenue.

steps.d: For a marketplace, use take_rate * GMV instead of monthly subscription, and compute CAC based on seller or buyer acquisition, not both.
For an online retailer, use (gross margin % * average order value) as the numerator in payback, not subscription revenue.
For each transaction type, calculate gross margin per transaction and CAC per transaction, then stack transactions per customer to estimate LTV.
If customers buy once, LTV = gross margin per transaction; if they repeat, LTV = (GM per transaction * expected repeats) - CAC.
Take your actual unit economics, identify the revenue model (SaaS, marketplace, e-commerce, ads), and compute CAC and LTV correctly for that model.

topics.title: Burn Rate & Runway
topics.description: Calculate gross and net burn rate, forecast your runway at the current spend trajectory, and identify the levers that extend it without killing growth.

steps.d: Gross burn = all operating expenses; net burn = gross burn - revenue; if spending $500k/month and earning $100k, net burn is $400k/month.
Divide current cash by monthly net burn to get months until zero cash; track this metric weekly so you know your funding timeline.
List ways to reduce burn (headcount, spend cuts, slower hiring) and ways to increase revenue (price increase, sales effort) and model impact of each.
Forecast runway under base case (current spending), aggressive case (cut 20% of burn), and conservative case (add 20% burn) to see range of outcomes.

steps.t: Present runway to leadership and investors
steps.d: Report months of runway remaining, the date the company runs out of cash at current burn, and which levers you'll use to extend it.

topics.title: Cash Flow Forecasting
topics.description: Build a 13-week cash forecast that tracks inflows and outflows at the transaction level — the model investors ask for when a startup is approaching the end of its runway.

steps.d: Create a weekly forecast of cash inflows (revenue, funding) and outflows (payroll, COGS, overhead) for 13 weeks to predict cash balance.
Track accounts receivable (money owed to you), accounts payable (money you owe), and inventory so the forecast reflects actual cash timing, not accrual revenue.
If payroll is due on the 15th but revenue comes on the 25th, show the resulting cash trough (low point) in week 2 and recovery in week 3.
As weeks close and new data arrives, replace forecast with actual and add a new week, keeping the rolling 13-week view current.
If the forecast shows a cash trough below zero in week 8, decide whether to collect receivables, delay payables, cut discretionary spend, or raise capital.

topics.title: Working Capital & Cash Efficiency
topics.description: Manage accounts receivable, payable, and inventory cycles to optimise cash timing — understand why profitable companies still run out of cash.

steps.d: Calculate Days Sales Outstanding (DSO): (accounts receivable / daily revenue); reduce by accelerating billing or payment terms, e.g. net 30 instead of net 45.
Extend Days Payable Outstanding (DPO) by negotiating longer terms with vendors or suppliers; moving from net 30 to net 45 frees up 15 days of cash.
Compute inventory turnover (COGS / average inventory); high turnover means less cash tied up; for retail, fast-moving items are better than slow.
CCC = DSO + DIO - DPO (days inventory outstanding); lower CCC means cash flows faster; optimize each component to minimize cash needs.

steps.t: Spot working capital as a lever
steps.d: Show that a $100k improvement in CCC (collect faster, pay slower, turn inventory quicker) can extend runway 2-3 weeks without raising capital.

topics.title: Startup Funding Stages
topics.description: Map the fundraising journey from angels and pre-seed through Series A, B, and C — understand what investors at each stage expect to see in traction and metrics.

steps.d: Describe the progression: angel/friends-family (pre-seed, $250k-1M), pre-seed ($500k-2M), seed ($2M-15M), Series A ($10M-50M), and later rounds, including typical investor focus at each.
Make a table that lists what VC investors look for at each stage (seed: early users; Series A: revenue and retention; Series B: unit economics), so you know what to prepare.
Assess whether your startup (product-market fit?, revenue?, growth rate?) should raise pre-seed, seed, or Series A and why.
Develop pitch deck, financial model, and metrics for your stage: seed focuses on vision and team, Series A on growth rate and market size.

steps.t: Evaluate whether to raise at your stage
steps.d: Decide whether raising capital now or waiting 6 months will give you better valuation and terms based on current runway and progress.

topics.title: Term Sheet Basics
topics.description: Decode the key provisions of a VC term sheet — valuation, liquidation preferences, pro-rata rights, anti-dilution clauses, and board composition.

steps.d: Explain that a $10M pre-money valuation means the company is worth $10M before investment; if you raise $5M at that valuation, post-money is $15M.

steps.t: Calculate founder proceeds at two exits
steps.d: For a startup with $5M raised at 1x non-participating preference, compute founder proceeds at a $20M exit (investors get $5M first, founders get $15M) and a $4M exit (investors get all $4M, founders get $0).
Broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution protects investors if a down round occurs; narrow-based affects founders more; understand which your term sheet uses.
Pro-rata rights let investors maintain their ownership % by participating in future rounds; understand which investors have this right.
Count board seats — founder, investor, independent — to see whether founders retain control or investors gain influence over key decisions.

topics.title: SAFEs & Convertible Notes
topics.description: Understand the mechanics of the Y Combinator SAFE and the convertible note — valuation caps, discount rates, and how they convert to equity at the next priced round.

steps.d: Read a sample SAFE document and locate the valuation cap (e.g., $10M) and discount rate (e.g., 20%), which determine the investor's conversion price at the next funding round.

Both convert to equity later; SAFEs have lower complexity and no interest, convertible notes have interest and explicit maturity, making notes riskier for investors but less dilutive upfront for founders.
If you raise on a SAFE with a $10M cap and later raise Series A at $20M valuation, the SAFE investor gets discount (e.g., 20% off) and converts at $16M valuation.
A lower cap favors investors (they get more shares); a higher cap favors founders; typical range is $3M-$10M for seed-stage; negotiate based on your progress.
Calculate fully diluted shares after converting all SAFEs and accounting for option pool; ensure founders understand their final ownership after multiple funding rounds.

topics.title: ARR, MRR & Churn
topics.description: Build ARR and MRR waterfalls showing new, expansion, contraction, and churn — the four components investors use to diagnose the health of a SaaS business.

steps.d: Build a monthly report showing: (opening ARR) + (new ARR from acquisition) - (churned ARR) + (expansion revenue from upsells) - (contraction revenue from downgrades) = (closing ARR).
Show each component separately so leadership sees which engine drives growth: new customer wins (fast-growing SaaS) or expansion (mature SaaS with land-and-expand).
MRR = ARR / 12; track monthly so you see monthly progress, then roll up to ARR for board reporting.
Monthly churn % = churned customers / starting customers; express as both $ churn rate (lost MRR / opening MRR) and logo churn (customer count lost).
Use your four components to forecast next quarter ARR: if new is up 20% and churn is flat, you'll grow; if new is down but expansion is strong, model the mix.

topics.title: Net Revenue Retention & Expansion
topics.description: Calculate net and gross revenue retention, understand why NRR above 100% creates compounding growth, and benchmark cohort retention against industry standards.

steps.d: For a cohort acquired in month 1, calculate what revenue persisted into month 2, 3, 4 with no new upsells; gross retention < 90% signals serious issues.
Calculate gross retention PLUS expansion revenue, so a cohort can have > 100% NRR if upsells exceed churn; NRR > 100% means the business compounds.
Compare retention curves across acquisition cohorts to see whether recent cohorts are better or worse than older cohorts; improving retention is a sign of product-market fit.
Show that NRR > 100% means efficient growth (expansion revenue funds new acquisition), while NRR < 100% requires external capital to grow.
Decide what gross and net retention your business needs to grow sustainably; for SaaS, > 95% gross and > 100% net retention are strong benchmarks.

topics.title: The SaaS Metrics Dashboard
topics.description: Assemble the metrics every SaaS board deck needs — ARR growth, NRR, LTV:CAC, payback period, Rule of 40, and magic number.

steps.d: Build a one-page dashboard showing ARR, ARR growth %, MRR churn, NRR, CAC, LTV:CAC, CAC payback period, and net dollar retention by cohort.
Show gross margin %, operating margin %, Rule of 40 (ARR growth % + operating margin %), and magic number (ARR growth / sales & marketing spend).
Track sales cycle length, win rate, average contract value, and renewal rate to see trends in sales execution.
Arrange metrics in a logical flow: growth (ARR, growth rate), quality (churn, NRR), capital efficiency (CAC, LTV, payback), and profitability (margins, Rule of 40).
Refresh the dashboard with actuals by month 5 of the close, present to leadership and board, and explain trends in each metric.

topics.title: Cap Table Structure
topics.description: Build a cap table from incorporation through multiple rounds — model how each new investment changes ownership percentages across founders, employees, and investors.

steps.d: Set up a spreadsheet showing founder shares (typically 10M common shares split 60/40 or equally) and calculate ownership %.
Add a seed investor who commits $2M at a $10M pre-money valuation; calculate post-money ($12M), investor shares (2M / 12M = 16.67%), and new founder ownership after dilution.
Reserve 10-15% of fully diluted shares for employee options; show how the pool is subtracted from founder shares before the seed investment.
Add a Series A: $10M at $30M pre-money; calculate new post-money, investor shares, and updated founder ownership after Series A dilutes them.
Show founder ownership declining with each round (common path: 100% → 70% after seed → 40% after Series A); calculate the total shares and ownership % for all parties.

topics.title: Employee Stock Options (ESOPs)
topics.description: Understand how option grants work — strike price, vesting schedules, cliff periods, exercise windows, and how to communicate equity value to candidates.

steps.d: Issue employee stock options with a strike price (typically the FMV at grant, often $0.01 for early hires) and a 4-year vest with a 1-year cliff.

steps.t: Calculate option value for a candidate
steps.d: For an employee granted 50k options at $0.01 strike, show them the potential value at different exit valuations ($100M = $2.5M per employee, $1B = $25M per employee).
Show that after 1 year, an employee is 25% vested; after 4 years, 100% vested; if they leave before 4 years, they forfeit unvested shares.
Track total options granted vs. pool size; if the pool is too small (< 5% remaining), board must approve an option pool expansion.
Calculate how the option pool affects fully-diluted share count for cap table and valuation purposes, so investors and founders understand true dilution.

topics.title: Dilution & Option Pool Shuffle
topics.description: Model dilution through new investment rounds, understand the option pool shuffle, and evaluate how liquidation preferences affect founder outcomes at exit.

steps.d: Show how founder ownership declines from round to round (seed, Series A, B, C) as new capital comes in; typical path ends at 20-30% founder ownership post-Series C.

Build a cap table showing how an option pool expansion before Series A prevents investor dilution; show the pool subtracted from founder shares before the new investor gets their %, so the investor's final ownership matches their negotiated percentage.
Model an exit at different valuations and show how proceeds are distributed: investors first (by preference), then option holders, then common shareholders (founders).
For a $100M exit, show how much each party nets after liquidation preferences; if investors have 1x non-participating, founders get all excess; if participating, they get less.

steps.t: Use cap table to guide fundraising
steps.d: Before raising the next round, model dilution and ask whether you're comfortable with the ownership impact; decide whether to raise less money or negotiate better terms.
